Mapagmahal St., Diliman, Quezon City OFFIC OF THE FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT 27_ s. 200-±_- 11 April 2008 MR. JOSE EDGARDO A. GOMEZ JR. ADB Consultant and SSL Team Leader No. 6, ADB Avenue Mandaluyong City Dear Mr. Gomez: This refers to your letter, endorsed by Mr. Victor B. Endriga, Quezon City Treasurer and the President of the Philippine Associations of Treasurers and Assessors (PHALTRA), requesting our legal opinion on whether Local Government Units (LGUs) can participate in the proposed Sub-Sovereign Lending (SSL) facility of the Asian Development Bank (ADB). Your letter was impelled by the existing DOJ and DILG Opinions discouraging LGUs from directly securing foreign loans pursuant to the provisions of Sections 301 and 297 or RA 7160, otherwise known as the Local Government Code of 1991 (LGC). You represented the following, among others: I. ADB is a multilateral finance institution created by a treaty to which the Philippines is party. 2. SSL is a lending facility being developed by ADB for LGUs, in which ADB will lend directly to LGUs either through direct loans or by purchasing LGU bonds. 3. SSL is a departure from the current practice of channeling multilateral agency funding through the National Government (NG) that in turn re-lends the funds to LGUs.

4. 5. 6. -2- SSL allows the National Government to reallocate to other critical uses resources that are currently devoted to processing on-lending facilities for LGUs. ADB will not require a direct guarantee from the National Government. This relieves the NG of the burden of incurring contingent liability and coincides with its debt stock reduction initiatives. ADB will lend to LGUs in Philippines Peso to eliminate foreign exchange risks for the LGUs. At the outset, please be informed that in conformity of the prevailing view, pursuant to a number of opinions issued by the Department of Justice and this Department (DILG Opinion Nos. 72-94; 145-03 and DOJ Opinion Nos. 39 s. 1997; 071 s. 1997; 062 s. 1998), LGUs cannot directly secure or contract foreign loans based principally on an interpretation of Section 301 in relation to Section 297 of the LGC. Nevertheless, taking into consideration the "personality" of ADB, to our mind, we have to understand first the sources of international law and delve into the relationship between an International Law and Municipal Law before we dispose of your request, thus: As to sources of international law Article 38 of the Statute of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) directs the Court to apply the following in deciding a case before it: a. international conventions, whether general or particular, establishing rules expressly recognized by the contesting States; b. international customs, as evidence of a general practice accepted as law; c. the general principles of law recognized by civilized nations; and d. subject to the provisions of Article 54, judicial decisions and the teachings of the most highly qualified publicists of the various nations, as subsidiary means for determination of rules of law.

-3- In conclusion, conformably to the Statute of the International Court of Justice, the primary sources of international law are as follows: I. 2. 3. International treaties or conventions; International customs; and General principles of law recognized by civilized nation. As to the relationship between an international law and municipal law: "There are two schools of tegaZ theory - dualist and monist - concerning the relationship between international and municipal Zaw. According to the dualist, international Zaw and municipal Zaw are two completely separate realms. Firstly, the sources of international Zaw are customs grown up among States and treaties concluded by them; the sources of municipal Zaw are custom and precedents grown up within the State's jurisdiction and legislation enacted by the State's lawmaking authority. Secondly, international law regulates relations between States, while municipal Zaw is concerned with individuals in their relations with each other and with the State. Thirdly, international law is not a taw above, but between sotereign States, whereas municipal Zaw is a Zaw of a sovereign over individuals subject to its authority. Hence, according to dualist theory, international law can net-er operate as the law of the land sate through or legislative municipal custom, judicial decision, enactment. There can, for example, be enabling legislation is required before the provision Of the treaty can be made operative upon persons within the State. In that event, the rules of international Zaw would become by adoption rules of municipal Zaw. The monist, on the other hand, deny that the subjects of the two systems of Zaw are essentially different and maintain that in both instances it is individual persons who in the ultimate analysis are regulated by the Zaw. Monistic doctrine asserts that international Zaw and municipal Zaw, far from being essentially different, must be regarded as parts of the same juristic conception. According to this doctrine, international Zaw is superior to municipal law; it is international Zaw which determines the jurisdictional limits of the personal and territorial competence of States." (Public

-4- International Law, 5th Edition by Salonga and Yap, pages IO- 11) Furthermore, in the jurisprudence of international tribunals, the principle of the supremacy of international obligations over national law has found repeated expression. For instance, the Permanent Court of International Justice held that "it is generally accepted principle of international Zaw that in the relations between Powers who are contracting Parties to a treaty, the provisions of municipal Zaw cannot prevail over those of the treaty." In another Advisory Opinion (Treatment of Polish National in Danzig), the same Court laid down that a State cannot adduce against another State its own constitution in order to evade obligations incumbent upon it under international law. Thus in the international sphere, a State is legally bound to observe its obligations under a treaty once it is duly signed and ratified in accordance with its constitutional system. (supra) Corollarilly, Article II of the Agreement Establishing the Asian Development Bank (ADB) provides, that: "Subject to the conditions stipulated in this Agreement, the Bank may provide or facilitate financing to any member, or any agency, instrumentality or political subdivision thereof, or any entity or enterprise operating in the territory of a member, as weZZ as to international or regional agencies or entities, concerned with economic development of the region. The Bank may carry out its operations in any of the following ways: (i) by making or participating in direct loans with its unimpaired paid-in capital and, except as provided in Article 17 of this Agreement, with its reserves and undistributed surplus; or with the unimpaired Special Funds resources; (ii) by making or participating in direct loans with funds raised by the Bank in capital markets or borrowed or otherwise acquired by the Bank for inclusion in its ordinary capital resources; xxx" Above premises considered, it seems to us that the subject treaty should be accorded great weight and respect. It should be treated the same as, if not, more that to our municipal laws or statutes. To us, the borrowing of LGUs with SSL of ADB is not within the contemplation of the

-5- "foreign loan" proscribed under Section 301 of the LGC for ADB has a charter that forms part of the Philippine laws, the latter being a signatory thereof. Therefore, based on the foregoing, it is our opinion that LGUs can participate in the proposed aforesaid SSL facility of the ADB. We hope to have answered your concern accordingly. Very truly yours, AUSTERE A. PANADER Undersecretar Legal/ O
